# 05. Kickoff Calls (The Leadership Kickoff)

Source: 8/19/2026 Rush Enterprises Leadership Kickoff (Lacy Buckingham Robertson, Marcelo Maceira; Grant, Olivia shadowing, Kaci Brown), ~31 minutes of a 60-minute booking. Citation tag **[kickoff]** = `transcripts/2026-08-19-rush/kickoff-leadership.md` (cite the timestamped body only; the file's header is engagement-repo analysis, not conversation). **[kickoff-agenda]** = `transcripts/2026-08-19-rush/kickoff-agenda-prep.md`, the internal agenda prepared two days ahead. Other tags as defined in module 00; **[go]** and **[delta-go]** carry the internal before-and-after of this call.

This module rests on one observed kickoff. Treat the shape as a first sketch; the Delta Water Products kickoff (week of 8/31) is the second data point and should be diffed against this the day its transcript lands.

## What a kickoff is for

Grant's own one-sentence purpose, said to the client in the first minute: "today is our kickoff call just to make sure we nail down our definitions of success and a point about InfoSec." **[kickoff 00:19]** Internally, the week before, he had put it as "to set our minimum and maximum definitions of success and just align on those things" **[kickoff-agenda]**, and on the Delta GO call he generalized the goal: "The goal of the kickoff call is to get as many quotes as possible as to how you're going to judge us. So we want to use those quotes over and over again." **[delta-go]** One more thing he tries to leave with: "one engagement-defining statement for the entire first project... And we want them to say yes." **[delta-go]**

So the kickoff produces three things, in priority order: the client's minimum and maximum definitions of success in their own words, a one-sentence statement of the engagement they have said yes to, and whatever mechanical decisions unblock the interview week (roster, survey audience, access). Everything else on the agenda is optional and, on the observed call, most of it did not survive contact with the clock.

The kickoff is pre-sold before the SOW exists. On the Delta data review call, asked "where do we go from here?", Grant's answer began with it: "our first step is a kickoff call where we're going to define our minimum and maximum definition of success. That way we are communicating throughout on how we're going to know if this was successful... Kickoff, 10 interviews, workflow assessment readout. That's it in a nutshell." **[delta-data 23:54, 26:27]** By the time the room arrives at the kickoff they have heard the two prompts once already, and the sponsor's pre-call document ("a lot of Madhav's questions in the email were really helpful for defining that") is the first draft.

## The lesson that came first: do not compress it

The observed kickoff was booked for an hour and Grant capped it himself: "we only have half an hour here today, and so I want to make sure that we get through our agenda." **[kickoff 04:03]** Five days later on the GO call he owned the result: "We got negative feedback on the kickoff call, which I will own for trying to rush that into a half hour. Lesson learned. We cannot rush kickoff calls into half an hour ever again, especially with large companies." **[go]** His diagnosis of why is worth keeping whole: "we are operating much faster than I think normal large companies are used to... where I think we can rush, we might not be able to rush where they expect us to do a lot." **[go]**

The agenda had six items sized to 45 minutes **[kickoff-agenda]**. The transcript shows two of them reached in full (definitions of success, InfoSec), one partially (roster), and the analytical items (mapping the readout onto the client's own AI framework, the survey window contradiction) never opened **[kickoff]**. The kickoff is the one session where the client should talk more than GPC, and that only happens with room.

## The shape of the observed call

Timestamps are from **[kickoff]**.

1. **Introduce the new faces, then state the purpose in one sentence.** "You're meeting a few more faces from GPC today, and so I figured it'd be useful to go around the room and just have a quick introduction from Olivia and Kaci... But, effectively, today is our kickoff call just to make sure we nail down our definitions of success and a point about InfoSec." [00:19] Olivia's own intro on this call was the shadow version: "I'm a workflow consultant. It just started a couple days ago, so this is my first shadowing call." [00:52] By 8/27 Grant introduces her as "another consultant on our team" **[sales]**; when she runs a kickoff herself, the intro should be the consultant version, not the shadow version.
2. **Clear the live item before the agenda.** Event points of contact and the status of the Jody asset took the first four minutes. [01:38 to 04:03] Grant also previewed a deliverable the client had not asked for: "we worked on that asset without you asking." [27:22] A kickoff opens with something moving.
3. **Walk the road.** Screen share up, then: "Where are we at in the journey? And what are our definitions of success?" [05:00] The walk names what is done ("a handful of calls with you and the team"), what today is for ("get all those communication, expectation management things out of the way... dropping off in this partnership from the best possible point"), who does what next ("Olivia will be shadowing me on those calls"), and the survey.
4. **Make the survey ask with the reasoning attached, then check.** He proposed the 190 event attendees rather than every employee and said why: "it'd be great to get it out to all employees... But I think that might ruffle some feathers in terms of, hey, here, take this survey, but where's the follow through?... How do you guys feel about that?" [05:00] Lacy's conditions came back immediately (review it first, get the raw data) and were answered in the moment: "Fully anonymous," the unique-ID trick (first name, first letter of mother's maiden name, birth year) so surveys can be paired without identifying anyone, and "we'll give you the raw data and the summaries, our analysis of it." [06:20 to 06:53] (Labels on this exchange are scrambled; attribution here is by substance.)
5. **Frame the minimum, and lower the stakes while raising the bar.** "I would be disappointed if GPC did not at least blank. It's a very easy sentence to finish for some people, somewhat complicated for others, but it's a good way for us to say, if we didn't do this, it's a failure, right? And so you can set this bar wherever you want... you could say, solve cancer. I'd say, all right, that's a heavy cross to bear, but let's give it a shot... what are your expectations and how do we know that we're going to hit them if we define them?" [07:00] The joke did work: twelve minutes later Marcelo handed it back ("It might be easier for you to find a cure for cancer than do all this") and Grant banked it ("we'll come back to it. I'll let you know in a few weeks"). [19:49 to 19:57]
6. **Expect a scope question, and answer it by splitting.** Before anyone answered, the room asked two clarifiers: is this for us or for the GMs, and is this the assessment or the whole engagement. [07:00, 09:05] Grant's split: "Let's separate it into the assessment of the interviews and the events as a separate thing... the fireside chat is a separate thing that we'll talk about a little bit later as we get closer to the event." [09:18] The lesson for the next kickoff is to say the scope and the answerers before asking, so the clarifier is not needed. If it comes anyway, answer it in one sentence; the Rush clarifier produced the most useful scope decision of the call.
7. **Open it to the room and let the long answers run.** Grant asked the room, not a person, and both sponsors answered in turn at length; Marcelo's maximum ran close to two minutes and carried a minimum inside it. [09:46 to 13:32] Nobody was cut off. The answers are the deliverable, so the time they take is the time the call is for. The observed ordering move for a bigger room comes from the interview panels, not from this call: announce the queue ("in the order that I see you on my screen") **[parts]**.
8. **Frame the maximum, and be ready to go first.** "you would tell everyone about us if we achieved blank. Not going to hold you to it, but it's still a good framing that how can we earn some sort of overwhelming rejoice of, man, these guys really crushed it. What would that look like? I have an idea, but Marcelo can go first." [12:18] Marcelo volleyed it back ("You got to go first now if you said it") and a model answer was delivered [12:54 to 12:59]; Fathom splits that sentence across two labels, so who spoke it is unresolved, but the move is clear: have a model maximum ready, offer to go first, and let the client build on it. Marcelo then did. [13:32]
9. **Reflect the answer back, credit the room, and say what it changes.** "Nice. Love that. I love the emphasis on, as Kaci pointed out too, the, what are your general manager, regional general manager, et cetera, expectations of the company? Almost bottom to top, right?... And this is exactly why I don't have a survey to show you in this call, because we want to customize it to these." [15:34] Three moves in one breath: restate the answer in a shape you can use, credit a teammate, and show the client their answer just changed the work. "There's no wrong answers with this. So this is my favorite part of the entire first week" [12:18] is the same posture from the other side.
10. **Ask the refining question that turns a wish into a deliverable.** "do you see us helping effectively write that company vision for AI based on the interviews? Is that one of the things that you would like us to write that sentence? Yep." [18:04] That is the engagement-defining statement from the GO call, obtained by asking for a yes. The client then said where it would be presented ("like you and Jodi on the stage"). [18:26]
11. **Say the goalposts can move.** "communication is what makes these types of partnerships... successful... just because it's today doesn't mean that you're not able to do that tomorrow. So if the goal changes, the goalposts change, or you want to add something to this list, just let us know, right? We're fluid. We're partners." [18:55]
12. **Ask where the end point is.** "Do you imagine at the end of this that there will be a presentation?... Will there also be a presentation to the board type of role, the rest of the C-suite?... just as far as understanding where the end point is?" [21:51] That single question surfaced "a board-ready roadmap that can be presented, whether or not you're involved" [22:26], which is a format constraint on the whole deliverable. Ask who sees the readout beyond the room, every time.
13. **What happens next, with the roster counted live.** Survey to them for confirmation, sent by their team; interviews next week; then the count: "I know that right now we have nine interviews on the calendar, if remember correctly. So we are missing one from the list. Lacy, did you end up combining the GMs or the RGMs?" [23:38] The hours flexibility line came in the same beat: "we haven't really hit a point in our engagements where 10 hours is not sufficient to give a roadmap, but with a company of your size and complexity, if you guys feel that there needs to be additional calls... It's just a conversation." [24:45]
14. **Set expectations from GPC's side, and own your own miss while doing it.** "the last thing that I wanted to bring up just today to make sure that I'm setting expectations from our side correctly is that... skills, connectors, these are table stakes." [26:04] Then, about the failed COO session: "to open up the settings and see that there were some missing pieces, it's like you can't even start the puzzle because all the corners are missing... obviously I didn't ask the right questions going into it and I've learned my lesson on that one... partnership goes both ways." [27:22] The kickoff is where GPC names what it needs from the client, and the credibility to do that comes from naming its own mistake first.
15. **Leave room for the client's late add.** With the call closing, Lacy raised training and continuous improvement: "I don't think we touched on that really much today." Grant absorbed it into the plan on the spot ("not today, but very much a part of our plan") and expanded it into AI onboarding and offboarding for new hires. [28:29 to 28:51] The thing the client raises at the end is often the thing they came for. Build an explicit "what haven't we covered?" beat before the close rather than relying on the client to interrupt.
16. **Close fast, and warmly.** "Productive 30 minutes. Thank you, everyone. Bye." [31:21]

## Patterns worth copying

- **Start from the onboarding form.** The closed-won automation sends a form (pain points, KPIs, minimum definition of success). "if we only have one person that fills this out, we can still take that information into the kickoff call and say, great, here's where we're jumping off from... Let's decompose it a little bit. Let's open it up a little bit, let it breathe, and talk through it." **[delta-go]** (Labels drift across this exchange; the posture is Grant's, flagged **[inferred]**.) The form answer is the first draft of the minimum, and the kickoff edits it out loud.
- **Enforce the form by client size.** "if they're smaller and we can boss them around... go fill out the form. When it's a publicly traded company, I'm going to give them a pass." **[delta-go]**
- **Put the client in the reflective seat before the call.** The Delta pre-kickoff email asked Madhav which brand to focus on: "just put them in the reflective seat before we have our kickoff call." **[delta-go]** A kickoff where the client has already thought about the hard question runs faster and produces better sentences.
- **Record it twice.** Both Grant and Olivia recorded the Rush kickoff (two Fathom IDs in the transcript header). With Fathom mislabelling speakers on 17 identified turns, the second recording is what makes a contested quote resolvable. Observed once; recommended as standing practice **[inferred]**.
- **Harvest the minimum that arrives inside the maximum.** Marcelo's fifth minimum (what the field expects of leadership) was delivered mid-way through his maximum and explicitly labelled as a minimum. [13:32] The capture doc needs a place for it, or it gets filed under the wrong heading and dropped.
- **Ask the client for their own test.** Marcelo's five questions (What is Rush's vision for AI? What does it mean for my role? How much am I expected to learn and use? What tools do I get? What am I expected to contribute back?) [16:25] arrived unprompted because the room had air. They are the most operationally useful sentence on the call, because anyone can run a finished deliverable against them. If a room does not volunteer its own test, ask for one: "at the end of this, what should any employee be able to answer?" **[inferred]** from this instance.
- **Listen for the tone constraint.** "not overhype, oversell. We definitely don't want to do that" [17:07] and "they're ignorant of AI and they don't know what they should even be afraid of... stigmas against utilizing AI" [20:02] are not definitions of success, but they fail the work if ignored. Capture constraints in the same doc as the definitions.
- **Do not attribute from the label.** See the transcript README. Every quote above that mattered was checked against the surrounding turns.

## Relationship to the other modules

- The GO call (module 02) sets the kickoff's target sentence and collects the quotes goal; the kickoff executes both.
- The same-day check-in (module 03) and the interview close (module 01) both reuse the definitions of success: the readout is measured against them, and the demo candidates are chosen to serve them.
- The kickoff deck itself is a GPC method artifact: seven slides, two of them blank fill-in-the-blank prompts for the minimum and the maximum, filled live and captured the same day. Its canon lives in the `gpc-skills` repo (`skills/kickoff-deck/references/kickoff-canon.md`) and is not reproduced here; this module documents what Grant actually did with it in the room.

One observed kickoff (Rush, 8/19), one internal retrospective on it (**[go]**), and one internal prep conversation for the next one (**[delta-go]**). The 60-minute shape is a recommendation derived from a 31-minute call that was judged too short by the person who ran it. The Delta kickoff transcript is the test.
